claim: Nearly every tumor type in TCGA contained samples where DNMT3B is upregulated.
source: our analysis showed that nearly every tumor type contained samples where DNMT3B is upregulated (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) (Duymich et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1A and cited literature.

claim: Within each cancer type, only a fraction of tumors overexpress DNMT3B, while many more acquire CGI hypermethylation.
source: However, within each cancer type, only a fraction of tumors overexpress DNMT3B, while many more acquire CGI hypermethylation (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B comparing DNMT3B overexpression to CGI hypermethylation incidence.

claim: The median CGI methylation level consistently increases across all cell and tissue types upon Dnmt3b induction.
source: Within a set of 7,467 CGIs covered in all samples, the median CGI methylation level consistently increases across all cell and tissue types, though both the percentage (6–15%) of hypermethylated CGIs and the average increase (2–9%) in mean CGI methylation vary upon Dnmt3b induction (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RRBS data analysis of 7,467 CGIs shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The percentage of hypermethylated CGIs varies from 6-15% upon Dnmt3b induction.
source: Within a set of 7,467 CGIs covered in all samples, the median CGI methylation level consistently increases across all cell and tissue types, though both the percentage (6–15%) of hypermethylated CGIs and the average increase (2–9%) in mean CGI methylation vary upon Dnmt3b induction (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of RRBS data across multiple tissues.

claim: The average increase in mean CGI methylation varies from 2-9% upon Dnmt3b induction.
source: Within a set of 7,467 CGIs covered in all samples, the median CGI methylation level consistently increases across all cell and tissue types, though both the percentage (6–15%) of hypermethylated CGIs and the average increase (2–9%) in mean CGI methylation vary upon Dnmt3b induction (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of RRBS data across multiple tissues.

claim: H3K36me3-enriched regions gained DNA methylation despite beginning at already high levels upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
source: Finally, we specifically looked at regions enriched for H3K36me3, which are known to recruit DNMT3B through its PWWP domain (Baubec et al., 2015; Dhayalan et al., 2010; Rondelet et al., 2016), and found that these regions also gained DNA methylation despite beginning at already high levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of H3K36me3-enriched regions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and cited literature on DNMT3B recruitment.

claim: 152/4,260 H3K36me3-enriched regions in kidney showed significant additional gain in methylation upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
source: In total, 152/4,260 and 222/9,824 H3K36me3-enriched regions showed significant additional gain in methylation (P-value <0.05, difference ≥0.2%, paired t-test) for kidney and liver respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of H3K36me3-enriched regions in kidney tissue.

claim: 222/9,824 H3K36me3-enriched regions in liver showed significant additional gain in methylation upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
source: In total, 152/4,260 and 222/9,824 H3K36me3-enriched regions showed significant additional gain in methylation (P-value <0.05, difference ≥0.2%, paired t-test) for kidney and liver respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of H3K36me3-enriched regions in liver tissue.

claim: A total of 4,839 differentially methylated CGIs were detected across intestine, liver, and kidney tissues upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
source: We did not observe any gross phenotypic changes in these tissues at the time of sample collection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), despite detecting a total of 4,839 differentially methylated CGIs across the three tissues (FDR q-value <0.05, methylation increase ≥0.2) from the 12,837 that were covered by RRBS (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RRBS analysis with statistical thresholds (FDR q-value <0.05, methylation increase ≥0.2).

claim: No gross phenotypic changes were observed in intestine, liver, and kidney tissues at the time of sample collection despite CGI hypermethylation.
source: We did not observe any gross phenotypic changes in these tissues at the time of sample collection (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), despite detecting a total of 4,839 differentially methylated CGIs across the three tissues (FDR q-value <0.05, methylation increase ≥0.2) from the 12,837 that were covered by RRBS (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological examination shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The gain at CGIs was highly reproducible between both technical and biological replicates.
source: The gain at CGIs was highly reproducible between both technical and biological replicates, suggesting a non-random increase at specific CGIs in each tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between replicates shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Roughly equal numbers of differentially methylated regions at CGIs were observed in intestine and liver, many of which were shared (n = 1,932).
source: We observed roughly equal numbers of differentially methylated regions (DMRs) at CGIs in intestine and liver, many of which were shared (n = 1,932).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of DMRs across tissues.

claim: The overall number of DMRs in kidney was lower than in intestine and liver, but a notable fraction was shared with the other two tissues.
source: The overall number in kidney was lower, but a notable fraction was also shared with the other two tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of DMRs across tissues shown in Figure 1D.

claim: More CGIs showed hypermethylation in HSCs and progenitor cells (HSC: n = 1,611, MPP: n = 1,117, CLP: n = 1,380) than in fully differentiated T cells (CD4+: n = 492, CD8+: n = 567).
source: More CGIs showed hypermethylation (q-value <0.05, methylation gain >0.3) in HSCs and progenitor cells (HSC: n = 1,611, MPP: n = 1,117, CLP: n = 1,380) than in fully differentiated T cells (CD4+: n = 492, CD8+: n = 567), although this may be associated with the relatively strict threshold as CD4+ and CD8+ cells appear to show less increase and already slightly higher baseline levels at targeted CGIs (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of hypermethylated CGIs across different blood cell types.

claim: DMRs were consistently enriched for the most lowly expressed genes.
source: DMRs were consistently enriched for the most lowly expressed genes, an overall trend that was maintained when gene promoters were divided into HCPs and LCPs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis correlating DMRs with gene expression levels shown in Figure 2D.

claim: De novo methylation through ectopic Dnmt3b occurs predominantly at the promoters of already silent/lowly expressed genes.
source: Nonetheless, we can conclude that de novo methylation through ectopic Dnmt3b occurs predominantly at the promoters of already silent/lowly expressed genes, which may explain both the shared and unique targets that we observed above.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression status and methylation patterns across multiple cell types.

claim: DMRs displayed significantly lower levels of H3K4me3 relative to non-DMRs at HCP and LCPs.
source: To explore this, we correlated the ectopic Dnmt3b RRBS data with H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 chromatin immunoprecipitation-sequencing (ChIP-seq) data of liver tissue from control mice and found that DMRs displayed significantly lower levels of H3K4me3 relative to non-DMRs at HCP and LCPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis comparing H3K4me3 levels at DMRs vs non-DMRs.

claim: HCPs that gained methylation had significantly higher H3K27me3 levels than non-DMR HCPs.
source: In contrast, HCPs that gained methylation had significantly higher H3K27me3 levels than non-DMR HCPs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis comparing H3K27me3 levels shown in Figure 3B.

claim: H3K27me3–only CGIs were much more likely to be hypermethylated than those that were bivalent or enriched for H3K4me3.
source: When we annotated all genomic CGIs by their chromatin state as H3K4me3, H3K27me3, both (bivalent) (Bernstein et al., 2006) or neither, and calculated the percentage of CGIs in each class that gained DNA methylation, we found that H3K27me3–only CGIs were much more likely to be hypermethylated than those that were bivalent or enriched for H3K4me3 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of CGI methylation stratified by chromatin state shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Using all features, the random forest classifier was able to recover 96.7% DMRs at a false discovery rate of 5%.
source: Using all features, we were able to recover 96.7% DMRs at a false discovery rate of 5%, demonstrating the high predictive impact of all features in combination (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by machine learning classification results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: H3K4me3, DNase and control methylation level displayed the greatest decrease in performance when removed from the DMR prediction model.
source: We next removed each parameter from the model in turn to assess its contribution to DMR detection, and noted that H3K4me3, DNase and control methylation level displayed the greatest decrease in performance (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by feature importance analysis from the random forest classifier shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CGIs with very low levels of methylation and enriched for H3K4me3 in open chromatin are the least susceptible to methylation gain.
source: As H3K4me3 and DNase signal are correlated with each other and anti-correlated with control methylation levels and H3K27me3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), this analysis shows that CGIs with very low levels of methylation and enriched for H3K4me3 in open chromatin are the least susceptible to methylation gain.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and feature importance from the prediction model.

claim: In ectopic Dnmt3b livers, there was no net effect on H3K4me3 at DMR promoters, but a depletion of H3K27me3.
source: Moreover, in the ectopic Dnmt3b livers, we found no net effect on H3K4me3 at DMR promoters, but a depletion of H3K27me3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq analysis comparing histone modifications before and after Dnmt3b induction shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Regions with H3K4me3 enrichment remain protected from gain of DNA methylation despite high levels of ectopic DNMT3B.
source: These dynamics suggest that regions with H3K4me3 enrichment remain protected from gain of DNA methylation despite high levels of ectopic DNMT3B, in agreement with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and RRBS data analysis and cited literature.

claim: Regions that have H3K27me3 are normally unmethylated, but are generally more susceptible to aberrant methylation.
source: In contrast, regions that have H3K27me3 are normally unmethylated, but are generally more susceptible to aberrant methylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of H3K27me3-marked regions and their methylation status.

claim: The overall number of hypermethylated CGIs in MEFs was comparable to in vivo samples (n = 908 and 3,160 for 1 and 7 d, respectively).
source: The overall number of hypermethylated CGIs was comparable to our in vivo samples (n = 908 and 3,160 for 1 and 7 d, respectively, FDR q-value <0.05 and gain of methylation ≥0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RRBS analysis of MEFs at two time points with statistical thresholds.

claim: Within one day of induction, a large number of CGIs gained methylation, and both the number and methylation level continued to increase after longer exposure.
source: Within one day of induction, a large number of CGIs gained methylation, and both the number and methylation level continued to increase after longer exposure (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course RRBS analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No genes from the highly expressed HCP-directed group with H3K4me3 gained methylation after 1 day, and only 1% showed any change in methylation after 7 days of induction.
source: Most highly expressed HCP-directed genes (2,378/2,485) were enriched for H3K4me3 and were generally protected from de novo methylation: no genes from this group gained methylation after 1 day, and only 1% showed any change in methylation after 7 days of induction.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of methylation changes at HCP promoters stratified by expression and chromatin state.

claim: Silent bivalent and K27me3-only HCPs were methylated early with 9% and 29% of loci on day 1 and 62% and 96% at day 7, respectively.
source: Alternatively, silent bivalent and K27me3-only HCPs were methylated early with 9% and 29% of loci on day 1 and 62% and 96% at day 7, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of methylation at HCPs with different chromatin states.

claim: For genes with neither H3K4me3 nor H3K27me3, 9% of highly expressed genes and 72% lowly expressed genes gained promoter methylation by day 7.
source: For genes with neither H3K4me3 nor H3K27me3, 9% of highly expressed genes and 72% lowly expressed genes gained promoter methylation by day 7.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of methylation changes at promoters without H3K4me3 or H3K27me3.

claim: Ectopic Dnmt3b is only able to target the promoters of lowly expressed genes, especially those enriched for H3K27me3.
source: These results strongly support our previous in vivo conclusions that ectopic Dnmt3b is only able to target the promoters of lowly expressed genes, especially those enriched for H3K27me3.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive analysis of methylation patterns in MEFs stratified by expression and chromatin state.

claim: H3K27me3-containing chromatin showed widespread gain of methylation at day 1 that increased to a higher level on day 7.
source: H3K27me3-containing chromatin showed widespread gain of methylation at day 1 that increased to a higher level on day 7 (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-BS-seq analysis shown in Figures 4D-F.

claim: DNMT3B can engage targets with H3K27me3 and methylate the surrounding DNA, which may eventually interfere with H3K27me3 maintenance and trigger its subsequent loss.
source: As such, DNMT3B can engage targets with H3K27me3 and methylate the surrounding DNA, which may eventually interfere with H3K27me3 maintenance and trigger its subsequent loss.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-BS-seq data showing co-occurrence of DNA methylation and H3K27me3 followed by H3K27me3 depletion.

claim: Only 39 genes were significantly downregulated and 13 genes were upregulated upon Dnmt3b overexpression in MEFs after 7 days.
source: Altogether, we saw only 39 genes that were significantly downregulated and 13 genes that were upregulated upon Dnmt3b overexpression (adjusted P-value <0.05, fold change >2), not including Dnmt3b itself.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis of MEFs after 7 days of Dnmt3b induction.

claim: The most highly upregulated gene was Rab6b, an oncogene, which was upregulated almost 4-fold upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
source: Interestingly, the most highly upregulated gene was Rab6b, an oncogene, which was upregulated almost 4-fold upon Dnmt3b overexpression.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis showing differential gene expression.

claim: Despite global H3K27me3 depletion, both Eed KD MEF lines still showed widespread CGI hypermethylation that increased to similar mean levels as prior control MEFs.
source: Nonetheless, despite global H3K27me3 depletion, both Eed KD MEF lines still showed widespread CGI hypermethylation that increased to similar mean levels as our prior control MEFs (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that PRC2 activity may not be essential for ectopic targeting in this context.
evidence: The claim is supported by RRBS analysis of Eed knockdown MEFs shown in Figure 4G.

claim: H3K27me3 and/or PRC2 are likely not required for inducing CGI hypermethylation in the ectopic Dnmt3b overexpression model.
source: Together, these findings suggest that H3K27me3 and/or PRC2 are likely not required for inducing CGI hypermethylation in this ectopic Dnmt3b overexpression model, although the complex or its modification appears essential for the targeting of selected CGIs in other contexts (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by Eed knockdown experiments and cited literature.

claim: The median methylation at the Uncx locus increased from 0.02 in control cells to 0.08 after 1 day of treatment, and to 0.18 after 7 days of treatment.
source: Consistent with previous results, we found a clear increase in DNA methylation at all CpG sites from day 1 to day 7, with median methylation at this locus increasing from 0.02 in the control cells to 0.08 after 1 day of treatment, and to 0.18 after 7 days of treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by ultra-deep bisulfite sequencing of the Uncx locus.

claim: The absence of highly methylated fragments argues against discrete cellular heterogeneity.
source: The absence of highly methylated fragments argues against discrete cellular heterogeneity.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of epiallele patterns from ultra-deep sequencing.

claim: Methylation is observed at multiple CpGs within the locus in each cell.
source: Rather, methylation is observed at multiple CpGs within the locus in each cell, as can be seen from the distribution of per-read (implying per-cell) methylation (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by per-read methylation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The total number of epialleles increased from 3,207 in the control cells to 14,469 (1 d) and to 16,915 (7 d).
source: The total number of epialleles increased from 3,207 in the control cells to 14,469 (1 d) and to 16,915 (7 d).
evidence: The claim is supported by epiallele counting from ultra-deep sequencing data.

claim: The number of epialleles increases substantially after the first day of treatment, but then seems to level off as methylation continues to increase.
source: It is interesting that the number of epialleles increases substantially after the first day of treatment, but then seems to level off as methylation continues to increase.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course analysis of epiallele diversity.

claim: Certain CpG sites within the locus appear more susceptible while others seemed resistant to methylation gain, with the percentage of reads methylated at each specific CpG varying from 2% to 54% across the sequence.
source: Indeed, certain CpG sites within the locus appear more susceptible while others seemed resistant to methylation gain, with the percentage of reads methylated at each specific CpG varying from 2% to 54% across the sequence.
evidence: The claim is supported by per-CpG methylation analysis from ultra-deep sequencing.

claim: Five consecutive CpG sites (#22 to #26) showed extremely low methylation level compared to other CpG sites in MEFs and in intestine and liver.
source: Five consecutive CpG sites (#22 to #26) showed extremely low methylation level compared to other CpG sites in MEFs (7 d) (Figure 5A), as well as in intestine and liver (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of specific CpG sites across multiple samples.

claim: These CpGs may remain hypomethylated due to the presence of transcription factor binding sites.
source: It appears, based on underlying motif analysis, that these CpGs may remain hypomethylated due to the presence of transcription factor binding sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Neighboring CpGs showed very little coordinated gain in methylation.
source: We therefore looked at the pairwise correlation of CpGs in phase within our amplicon sequencing reads as a function of the genomic distance between them (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and observed low correlation levels (maximum 0.37), with neighboring CpGs showing very little coordinated gain in methylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pairwise correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DNMT3B may act focally at each CpG, either by distributive association/dissociation with the DNA, or by a processive (continuous) walk with skipping of CpGs along its path.
source: This indicates that DNMT3B may act focally at each CpG, either by distributive association/dissociation with the DNA, or by a processive (continuous) walk with skipping of CpGs along its path.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the low correlation between neighboring CpGs.

claim: CGI shores have previously been shown to be hypermethylated in cancers.
source: CGI shores have previously been shown to be hypermethylated in cancers (Irizarry et al., 2009) and we found several orthologous human tumor suppressor genes or biomarkers that gained methylation at promoter-proximal CGIs and shores when Dnmt3b was overexpressed in mouse tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The genome-wide results confirm a selected subset of targets that was previously reported in the context of ectopic Dnmt3b expression in APCmin mice.
source: Our genome-wide results also confirm a selected subset of targets that was previously reported in the context of ectopic Dnmt3b expression in APCmin mice, which lead to an increase in adenoma formation (Linhart et al., 2007) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published data and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The majority of bivalent (81%) and H3K27me3-only (93%) CGIs are targeted by ectopic Dnmt3b in mouse B cells.
source: However, upon closer inspection of mouse control and Dnmt3b overexpressing B cells to human normal B cells and CLL, we see that the majority of bivalent (81%) and H3K27me3-only (93%) CGIs are targeted by ectopic Dnmt3b, while only 12% and 21% are targeted in CLL, rendering the overlap high, but significance low (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only 12% of bivalent and 21% of H3K27me3-only CGIs are targeted in CLL.
source: However, upon closer inspection of mouse control and Dnmt3b overexpressing B cells to human normal B cells and CLL, we see that the majority of bivalent (81%) and H3K27me3-only (93%) CGIs are targeted by ectopic Dnmt3b, while only 12% and 21% are targeted in CLL, rendering the overlap high, but significance low (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The ectopic system methylates a large proportion of cancer targets (84% orthologous CLL CGIs in total).
source: Overall, we conclude that even though the ectopic system methylates a large proportion of cancer targets (84% orthologous CLL CGIs in total), this may in part be due to the high expression levels of Dnmt3b rather than a shared mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of methylation targets between the ectopic system and CLL.

claim: The ectopic system showed an overall increase in methylation at 100 bp tiles regardless of the original methylation level.
source: Furthermore, while our system showed an overall increase in methylation at 100 bp tiles regardless of the original methylation level (but highest for tiles with low to intermediate original methylation), the distribution of methylation changes in colorectal cancer (TCGA) showed similar increases at lowly methylated genomic regions, but a loss of methylation at intermediate and highly methylated genomic regions, in keeping with the general global hypomethylation reported in cancer (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of methylation changes at 100 bp tiles shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The distribution of methylation changes in colorectal cancer showed similar increases at lowly methylated genomic regions, but a loss of methylation at intermediate and highly methylated genomic regions.
source: Furthermore, while our system showed an overall increase in methylation at 100 bp tiles regardless of the original methylation level (but highest for tiles with low to intermediate original methylation), the distribution of methylation changes in colorectal cancer (TCGA) showed similar increases at lowly methylated genomic regions, but a loss of methylation at intermediate and highly methylated genomic regions, in keeping with the general global hypomethylation reported in cancer (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA colorectal cancer data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ectopic system shares some common targets and possible mechanisms with human cancer, including preferential targeting of CGIs that have H3K27me3 or bivalent chromatin.
source: Together, these features suggest that our ectopic system shares some common targets and possible mechanisms with human cancer, including preferential targeting of CGIs that have H3K27me3 or bivalent chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative analysis of methylation targets between the ectopic system and human cancers.

claim: The ectopic system does not fully recapitulate the global methylation trends that characterize the cancer methylome.
source: However, it does not fully recapitulate the global methylation trends that characterize the cancer methylome.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of global methylation patterns between the ectopic system and cancer.

claim: DNMT3B preferentially targets CGIs near silent gene promoters, which tend to be enriched for H3K27me3.
source: Specifically, we found that DNMT3B preferentially targets CGIs near silent gene promoters, which tend to be enriched for H3K27me3, a repressive histone modification catalyzed by PRC2.
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive analysis of methylation targets and their chromatin states.

claim: De novo methylation by ectopically expressed Dnmt3b can transiently co-exist with H3K27me3-modified histones.
source: Our results also show that de novo methylation by ectopically expressed Dnmt3b can transiently co-exist with H3K27me3-modified histones, although H3K27me3 appears to be lost as DNA methylation continues to increase, which raises some interesting and mechanistically relevant questions.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-BS-seq data showing co-occurrence of DNA methylation and H3K27me3.

claim: H3K27me3 appears to be lost as DNA methylation continues to increase.
source: Our results also show that de novo methylation by ectopically expressed Dnmt3b can transiently co-exist with H3K27me3-modified histones, although H3K27me3 appears to be lost as DNA methylation continues to increase, which raises some interesting and mechanistically relevant questions.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course ChIP-BS-seq data.

claim: The majority of CpGs in mammalian genomes are methylated.
source: While the majority of CpGs in mammalian genomes are methylated, clusters of CpGs called CpG islands (CGIs) remain generally unmethylated, and are often located near or within housekeeping and developmental gene promoters (Bird, 1986; Saxonov et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNA methylation patterns.

claim: Clusters of CpGs called CpG islands (CGIs) remain generally unmethylated.
source: While the majority of CpGs in mammalian genomes are methylated, clusters of CpGs called CpG islands (CGIs) remain generally unmethylated, and are often located near or within housekeeping and developmental gene promoters (Bird, 1986; Saxonov et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on CpG island characteristics.

claim: CGIs are often located near or within housekeeping and developmental gene promoters.
source: While the majority of CpGs in mammalian genomes are methylated, clusters of CpGs called CpG islands (CGIs) remain generally unmethylated, and are often located near or within housekeeping and developmental gene promoters (Bird, 1986; Saxonov et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on CpG island genomic locations.

claim: Pre-existing methylation patterns are propagated by the maintenance DNA methyltransferase DNMT1.
source: Pre-existing methylation patterns are propagated by the maintenance DNA methyltransferase DNMT1, and new modifications are generally added by the de novo methyltransferases DNMT3A and 3B (Bestor, 2000; Charlton et al., 2018; Denis et al., 2011; Jeltsch, 2002; Xu and Corces, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT1 function.

claim: New modifications are generally added by the de novo methyltransferases DNMT3A and 3B.
source: Pre-existing methylation patterns are propagated by the maintenance DNA methyltransferase DNMT1, and new modifications are generally added by the de novo methyltransferases DNMT3A and 3B (Bestor, 2000; Charlton et al., 2018; Denis et al., 2011; Jeltsch, 2002; Xu and Corces, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT3A and DNMT3B function.

claim: Loss of Dnmt1 and Dnmt3b in mice causes prenatal lethality.
source: Loss of these enzymes in mice causes prenatal (Dnmt1 and Dnmt3b) or postnatal (Dnmt3a) lethality, which underscores their essential role in mammalian development (Li et al., 1992; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT knockout phenotypes.

claim: Loss of Dnmt3a in mice causes postnatal lethality.
source: Loss of these enzymes in mice causes prenatal (Dnmt1 and Dnmt3b) or postnatal (Dnmt3a) lethality, which underscores their essential role in mammalian development (Li et al., 1992; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT knockout phenotypes.

claim: DNMT3A and DNMT3B are structurally similar and appear to have redundant functions overall.
source: DNMT3A and DNMT3B are structurally similar and appear to have redundant functions overall, although the knockout phenotypes are distinct and some specific targets are well established for DNMT3B, such as pericentromeric repeats and germline gene promoters (Liao et al., 2015; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT3A and DNMT3B structure and function.

claim: Some specific targets are well established for DNMT3B, such as pericentromeric repeats and germline gene promoters.
source: DNMT3A and DNMT3B are structurally similar and appear to have redundant functions overall, although the knockout phenotypes are distinct and some specific targets are well established for DNMT3B, such as pericentromeric repeats and germline gene promoters (Liao et al., 2015; Okano et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT3B-specific targets.

claim: Both DNMT3A and DNMT3B are highly expressed in early embryos.
source: Both enzymes are highly expressed in early embryos, but only DNMT3A remains active in the adult and appears to be the major de novo methyltransferase involved in dynamic regulation of DNA methylation in somatic lineages (Ziller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT expression patterns.

claim: Only DNMT3A remains active in the adult and appears to be the major de novo methyltransferase involved in dynamic regulation of DNA methylation in somatic lineages.
source: Both enzymes are highly expressed in early embryos, but only DNMT3A remains active in the adult and appears to be the major de novo methyltransferase involved in dynamic regulation of DNA methylation in somatic lineages (Ziller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT3A function in adult tissues.

claim: Levels of catalytically active DNMT3B decrease sharply during pluripotent stem cell differentiation as cells switch to an inactive isoform.
source: In contrast, levels of catalytically active DNMT3B decrease sharply during pluripotent stem cell differentiation as cells switch to an inactive isoform (Gifford et al., 2013; Gordon et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT3B isoform switching during differentiation.

claim: Deregulation of all three catalytically active human DNA methyltransferases is found across a wide range of diseases.
source: In fact, deregulation of all three catalytically active human DNA methyltransferases is found across a wide range of diseases (Hamidi et al., 2015; Robertson, 2005) and mutations in both regulatory and catalytic domains are known contributing factors (Jin et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2011; Winkelmann et al., 2012; Xu et al., 1999; Yan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT deregulation in disease.

claim: Mutations in both regulatory and catalytic domains of DNMTs are known contributing factors to disease.
source: In fact, deregulation of all three catalytically active human DNA methyltransferases is found across a wide range of diseases (Hamidi et al., 2015; Robertson, 2005) and mutations in both regulatory and catalytic domains are known contributing factors (Jin et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2011; Winkelmann et al., 2012; Xu et al., 1999; Yan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT mutations in disease.

claim: Evidence exists that overexpression of DNMTs, especially DNMT3B, correlates with the epigenetic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and tumor formation.
source: Although evidence exists that overexpression of DNMTs, especially DNMT3B, correlates with the epigenetic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and tumor formation, primary tumors accrue substantial CGI methylation while the global average decays, and without temporal analysis, it cannot be ascertained whether global and local misregulation co-occur or if they represent distinct regulatory modes that arise independently (Baylin and Jones, 2011; Ben Gacem et al., 2012; Butcher and Rodenhiser, 2007; Girault et al., 2003; Portela and Esteller, 2010; Roll et al., 2008; Steine et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on DNMT overexpression in cancer.

claim: CGIs that gained DNA methylation in a colon cancer cell line were depleted of H3K27me3.
source: CGIs that gained DNA methylation in a colon cancer cell line were depleted of H3K27me3 and switching from H3K27me3 to DNA hypermethylation was also observed at silenced gene promoters in human prostate cancer cells (Brinkman et al., 2012; Gal-Yam et al., 2008; Statham et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on H3K27me3 and DNA methylation in cancer cell lines.
